US stocks fell suddenly on Thursday as AI and chip stocks sold off, erasing the gains from Wednesday's post-election rally.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ) tumbled 2.2%, or over 1,200 points. The S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) fell 3.3%, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) dropped 5%, putting the index on track to close in a correction.
The PHLX Semiconductor index ( ^SOX ) dived 11% as Nvidia ( NVDA ), Micron ( MU ), and other chip names sank.
Investors continued to process the Democrats' sweeping victory on Tuesday and its implications for markets and the economy . Amid relief that election uncertainty has been removed, the stock market continues to sort out the perceived winners and losers of a regime change on Capitol Hill.
Oil prices rose amid uncertainty that President Trump would pursue a deal with Iran to end the war in the Middle East. Optimism grew overnight after Vice President JD Vance said, "The reason we lost [the midterm elections] is the war," in a post on X suggesting the party should push for a resolution to the conflict. Brent crude oil ( BZ=F ) prices traded around $97 per barrel, while US benchmark WTI crude ( CL=F ) stood at $90 per barrel.
A report from Challenger, Gray & Christmas showed layoff plans in October fell to the lowest level since 2023 as companies turned their attention to retaining existing employees, setting the scene for Friday's key employment report.
On the earnings calendar, Duke Energy ( DUK ), Airbnb ( ABNB ), and Lumentum ( LITE ), among others, report results.
Bitcoin ( BTC-USD ) tumbled below $76,000 on Thursday as a broad sell-off in US stocks threatened to erase the previous day's post-election rally.
The world's largest cryptocurrency fell more than 5% Thursday, reversing a sharp rebound Wednesday that had lifted bitcoin above $80,000 as investors cheered midterm election results showing Democrats swept both chambers of Congress. The move has followed major indexes shedding their Wednesday gains.
Bitcoin's retreat also underscored of the crypto market's lingering fragility following $6.3 billion hack of Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, which rattled crypto prices last week.
The Democratic takeover of Congress also has raised fresh questions the crypto industry's prospects in Washington, including passage of the industry's long-stalled bill, the Clarity Act.
Brian Gardner, Stifel's chief Washington policy strategist, said in a briefing with reporters on Thursday that the Clarity Act is unlikely to advance before the end of the year.
"It's off the table for the lame duck session," Gardner said, adding that the odds of a bipartisan compromise in the next Congress are "pretty low."
Gardner added that he expects Senator Elizabeth Warren, who is poised to chair the Senate Banking Committee, to pursue investigations targeting crypto firms along with Wall Street banks and private equity firms.
Stocks began diving on Thursday morning as chip stocks sold off, erasing roughly $2 trillion in market cap and reversing the gains made in yesterday's post-election rally.
The Nasdaq fell roughly 4%, the S&P 500 dropped 2.3%, and the Dow shed over 700 points, or 1.4%.
Nvidia ( NVDA ), Micron ( MU ), and AMD ( AMD ) fell over 6%, 12%, and 13%, respectively.

US stocks were mixed Thursday as Wednesday's post-election stock rally began to fade, tech stocks came under renewed pressure, and oil prices rebounded.

Chip and data-center stocks were among the biggest laggards as investors continued to weigh what the Democratic sweep could mean for AI infrastructure spending and regulation. Qualcomm ( QCOM ) also sank after its quarterly results.
Oil prices bounced after Wednesday's sharp sell-off, with Brent crude prices ( BZ=F ) climbing back above $97 per barrel.
AppLovin ( APP ) shares surged 23% in premarket trading on Thursday after the mobile app marketing company posted better-than-expected third-quarter profit and revenue and issued upbeat fourth-quarter guidance. Wall Street analysts raised their price target on the stock as results eased concerns over the company's growth trajectory.
AppLovin's third-quarter revenue of $2.18 billion topped analyst expectations of $2.07 billion, according to Bloomberg estimates.
Earnings per share came in at $4.30, ahead of the $4.04 consensus estimate. AppLovin issued a stronger-than-expected fourth-quarter forecast, projecting revenue between $2.37 billion and $2.40 billion, well above the $2.25 billion analysts had anticipated.
Wall Street analysts were quick to upgrade the stock, with BTIG raising its price target to $450 from $396 while maintaining a Buy rating, implying approximately 35% upside from current levels. Needham also reiterated its Buy rating with a $475 price target, implying an upside of roughly 43%

"The Independent Committee thoroughly evaluated this Proposal and unanimously concluded that it substantially undervalues Wendy's standalone prospects and long-term earnings potential," Wendy's board chair Art Winkleblack wrote in a statement . "Our confidence rests firmly in Bob Wright's proven track record of seasoned industry leadership, including restaurant business turnarounds."
Wendy's separately announced a multiyear strategic turnaround plan, called Dave's Way, as it looks to stem declining sales and franchisees closing their locations.
The stock rose 1.5% in premarket trading.
The Bank of England (BOE) voted 8-1 to raise interest rates by a quarter point to 4% on Thursday, with one member dissenting in favor of a larger hike. It marked the first interest rate hike by the UK's central bank since 2023.
The bank sees inflation rising to 5% by mid 2027, and those inflationary pressures prompted the BOE to move.
"Today's increase shouldn't be seen as the first in an inevitable long sequence of hikes," BOE Governor Andrew Bailey said. "But unless the conflict in the Middle East is resolved, neither does it seem likely to be the last increase."

articles.content_orig:
First lady Melania Trump will host representatives from Russia and Ukraine at the White House on Thursday, her latest diplomatic initiative after an unprecedented humanitarian ceasefire she helped broker between the warring sides.
The meeting comes as the Trump administration pushes for progress in broader peace negotiations, with the United States set to lead renewed trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, next week. The losses suffered by Republicans in the midterm elections dealt a setback to President Donald Trump and his foreign policy, injecting yet more uncertainty into the American approach to the conflict.
“This event represents an extraordinary moment in American history,” the White House said in a statement announcing Thursday’s meeting.
It appears that this will be the first time both sides will meet face-to-face at the White House. It is unclear what exactly the gathering was designed to achieve and whether the president or any of his envoys would attend.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
President Vladimir Putin’s special envoy Kirill Dmitriev and human rights commissioner Yana Lantratova, who coordinated the humanitarian ceasefire on the Russian side, were expected to represent Russia at the gathering, according to the Kremlin.
Ukraine has not officially confirmed who will attend the meeting from its side, but the head of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s ruling faction in parliament, David Arakhamia, will be part of the country’s delegation, his office told NBC News, signaling that attendees would be high-level officials.
The gathering comes as Trump ramped up pressure on Kyiv and agreed on deals with the Kremlin in a bid to break a monthslong deadlock in negotiations to settle the war.
Those efforts were boosted by the humanitarian truce, which started Oct. 27 and lasted six days , allowing for the evacuation of hundreds of people from Oleshky. The town in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region was home to some 2,000 remaining residents on the brink of starvation.
Both sides held fire throughout the truce, making it the largest de-escalation effort since Russia’s full-scale invasion in early 2022.
“This achievement marks an unprecedented diplomatic initiative by an American First Lady,” the White House said Tuesday of the ceasefire.
Pope Leo XIV and some officials in Europe also lobbied heavily for the ceasefire in Oleshky.
On Wednesday, Ukraine bestowed a state award on Melania Trump for “significant personal contribution to humanitarian support for Ukraine.”  The Order of Princess Olga, 1st class is an honor for women who have made an outstanding contribution to the country.
Ukraine has been reeling from the worst collapse in relations with Washington since the start of the war. Trump signed a deal to buy Russian diesel and waived new sanctions on Moscow last month, while Kyiv complained of gaps in U.S. intelligence sharing and the slowdown of tech billionaire Elon Musk’s Starlink service , crucial for Ukraine’s military and air defense.
Ukraine has since said that both intelligence sharing and Starlink service have been restored, and that it was looking forward to resuming trilateral talks with the U.S. and Russia next week.
“This will be a team-level format, and we count on the work in this format and our other diplomatic steps opening the way to a trilateral format at the leaders’ level,” Zelenskyy said Tuesday. “It is precisely such a format — at the leaders’ level — that can resolve the key issues in order to achieve a lasting peace and guaranteed security.”
The meeting comes after Democrats captured full control of Congress in a striking repudiation of Trump’s agenda.
Kremlin said it “sincerely hoped” that Trump would continue his “peace-building efforts” after the midterm elections. Ukraine offered no official response to the dramatic results, but some in the country expressed cautious optimism the Democratic surge would ease pressure from Washington.
The negotiations to settle the war, led by Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner, have stalled over the key question of Ukraine’s eastern Donbas industrial region, which Putin wants to seize in its entirety.
Ukraine still controls key stronghold cities in the Donbas and has refused to give up this land, arguing Putin may be eyeing not just a public relations success but a powerful launchpad for future invasion attempts.
Yuliya Talmazan is a reporter for NBC News Digital, based in London.

articles.title_orig: China’s Moonshot AI seeks Nvidia Blackwell access in Europe, CNBC reports
articles.title_zh: China’s Moonshot AI seeks Nvidia Blackwell access in Europe, CNBC reports
articles.content_orig:
Moonshot AI, a Chinese artificial intelligence lab that the White House accused of accessing Nvidia advanced chips remotely in East Asia, has sought access to the chips through data centers in Europe, sources have told CNBC.
Deals have been discussed this year for Moonshot to rent capacity from neoclouds hosting Nvidia graphics processing units, or GPUs, at facilities in Europe, four people familiar with the matter said. They asked not to be named because they were discussing private information.
Nvidia's effective monopoly over the most powerful chips has made U.S. export controls a key tool in Washington's effort to preserve its advantage over China in the AI race. American AI labs such as OpenAI and Anthropic are locked in a training and pricing battle with Chinese developers, including Moonshot AI, which makes the Kimi family of models.
Moonshot was looking to lease capacity powered by Nvidia's Blackwell systems, advanced chips currently subject to those export controls which effectively ban their import into China, three of the sources told CNBC.
In July, the White House said the Chinese AI lab had accessed Nvidia's Blackwell chips via a facility in Thailand.
U.S. export controls restrict the shipment of Nvidia's most advanced chips to China, but remote access via overseas data centers offers a loophole. Current law does not give regulators broad authority to control companies' access to those chips through cloud services hosted overseas.
Moonshot, Nvidia, the White House, the U.S. Department of Commerce, China's embassy in the U.K. and its Ministry of Foreign Affairs did not respond to a request for comment.
Chinese developers have made notable capability gains in the past six months and greater access to Nvidia chips could put even more pressure on their American rivals.
To lease Nvidia computing power in Europe, a Chinese AI company would typically rent capacity from a non-Chinese neocloud or data center operator that can purchase advanced chips.
Moonshot was interested in leasing capacity on clusters for inference, which refers to serving models to end users, in Europe, two of the sources said. One of the sources said they were also aware of interest in clusters for training.
Talks for arrangements that would see Moonshot rent access to clusters of 8,000 or more Blackwell GPUs hosted in the region have taken place, one source said. They described the Chinese AI lab as "very aggressive" in its pursuit of more computing power.
One of the sources told CNBC that talks on securing Moonshot compute in Europe had taken place since the White House said it had done so via Thailand. Moonshot did not comment at the time.
Founded in 2023, Beijing-based Moonshot AI is one of China's leading model builders. It released a new model in July that Moonshot said closed the gap with leading systems built by Anthropic and OpenAI.
The model saw significant uptake as a cheaper alternative to U.S. offerings. Chinese AI models have surged in global adoption in 2026 , amid capability gains and lower costs than U.S. rivals.
Around the time Kimi K3 was released, Moonshot said demand had stretched its capacity, and it temporarily paused new subscriptions to prioritize compute for current members. "We're adding capacity as fast as we can and will reopen new subscription spots in batches," the company said in a LinkedIn post.
Leasing AI compute is a booming industry, with customers, or offtakers, typically taking capacity for a fee and paying an upfront cost to secure the deal, which is a percentage of the lifetime contract value.
One source said it had been proposed that Moonshot pay 30% to 50% more upfront than a non-Chinese offtaker would.
Arrangements with Chinese customers can be more lucrative upfront, as neoclouds and financing firms look to hedge against a potential future ban of remote access agreements.
In Washington, lawmakers have proposed the Remote Access Security Act (RASA) to expand U.S. export controls to include the cloud-based access of critical hardware and software. It passed the House of Representatives in January but has not passed the Senate.
The Financial Times reported on Tuesday that the chip giant told cloud providers selling access to their chips that they must sell at least 51% of services to non-Chinese customers.
Asked about the reports earlier this week, an Nvidia spokesperson said: "America cannot win the AI race unless America's AI infrastructure wins worldwide — if the world's clouds rely on foreign-made chips, the model and application layers will be foreign-built as well."
Nvidia said in August that Washington had licensed some sales of its H200 AI chips, an older generation, but that "such sales were restricted" by the Chinese government, which has sought to boost domestic chipmakers by limiting access to Nvidia chips.

articles.title_orig: The US Midterm Elections: Views From China - The Diplomat
articles.title_zh: The US Midterm Elections: Views From China - The Diplomat
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. midterm elections on November 3 were closely watched around the world as a way to gauge public support for the polarizing administration of Donald Trump. The verdict is in: the opposition Democratic Party won big, taking control of both houses of Congress with majorities Democrats haven’t enjoyed in years. Several states elected Democratic senators and governors for the first time in decades – in some cases, nearly a century .
Officially, of course, China won’t comment on the results of the election. That, as Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told reporters on November 4, is “a domestic affair” of the United States. “China stands ready to continue working with the U.S. to uphold and deliver on the important common understandings reached by the two heads of state,” Mao said.
In a speech delivered on election day, Xie Feng, China’s ambassador to the United States, said , “A confident and composed China is committed to the steady, sound, and sustainable development of China-U.S. relations… China’s policy toward the United States remains consistent and stable.”
The first news readouts from Xinhua, China’s state news agency, were also terse, although the points of information they chose to include were telling. In one early article , for example, Xinhua did not mention the historic nature of Democratic Party wins, but instead quoted Trump’s social media post that “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!” The short, three-paragraph report also devoted the entire last paragraph to comments from a White House official, who predicted U.S. voters “will suffer from severe buyer’s remorse.”
Xinhua published a much longer analysis on November 4, highlighting four “unexpected” outcomes. This article delved into the massive scale of the Democratic victory, from the size of its new House majority to the flipping of Senate seats in traditionally safe Republican states like Texas, Iowa, Kansas, and South Carolina.
Rather than offering perspectives from Chinese analysts, Xinhua’s article extensively cited U.S. media, including this quote from the Wall Street Journal : “Rarely in American politics has a president traded away so much political support so quickly. The losses that Republicans suffered on Tuesday marked one of the most decisive repudiations of a president in modern history.”
Chinese state media had much less to say about the causes of the Republican defeat – again, Beijing’s official line being that this is an “internal affair” of the United States. However, Xinhua did cite the general thesis by U.S. analysts that economic dissatisfaction amid rising prices was the primary culprit. And those rising prices were exacerbated by the Trump administration’s decision to strike Iran. Xinhua published a whole article covering Vice President J.D. Vance’s post-election verdict that the war on Iran had cost the Republicans control of Congress.
One Xinhua report cited Iran’s Speaker of Parliament Mohammad Ghalibaf, who posted on X : “Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message.”
“What the Chinese public is most concerned about … is the impact of the U.S. midterm election results on the Iran war and Ukraine war,” Mu Chunshan, an independent political analysts based in Beijing, told The Diplomat via email. “They are less focused on the impact on China-U.S. relations. This is because Trump has consistently shown respect to China.”
If Democrats act to restrain Trump’s military operations in Iran, Mu said, it would be align “with China’s long-standing call for a peaceful resolution of the Iran nuclear issue.” He sees the election results as “conducive to China and other countries pushing for a negotiated resolution of the Iran nuclear issue and Strait [of Hormuz] security issues.”
That said, Chinese analysts are well aware of Congress’ limited control over foreign policy. In an pre-election analysis, South China Morning Post cited Zhao Zhijiang , a research assistant at the Beijing-based independent think tank Anbound, as predicting that “Diplomacy may become even more transactional. U.S. policy towards Russia, Iran, Europe and China could swing rapidly between heavy pressuring and partial bargaining.” In other words, China is bracing for impact as a notoriously mercurial leader feels increased political pressure at home.
Diao Daming, an international relations professor at Renmin University in Beijing, told SCMP Trump might become more “legacy-driven” in his pursuit of foreign policy.  “On the other hand, in areas he believes he can control or achieve results quickly, he may also take some risky actions,” Diao said.
With a Trump-Xi summit looming later this month, China will be one of the first to get a feel for how the midterm defeat impacts Trump’s foreign policy style. China is hosting the APEC Leaders’ Meeting from November 18-19, with Trump expected to attend. Beside yet another summit between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping – the third in 2026 alone – there has been much discussion of other potential sideline meetings, including a possible China-Russia-U.S. trilateral.
China had its own reasons to be skeptical about hosting such a meeting . After the midterm outcomes, which will likely result in increased congressional support for Ukraine, there’s even less reason for Beijing to look positively on the prospects of a Putin-Trump-Xi meeting.
“At the APEC summit, if China, the US and Russia hold a trilateral summit, there is a high probability that the Ukraine war will not be discussed, because the midterm results make it harder for Trump to pressure Ukraine into accepting a ‘land-for-peace’ plan.” Mu said. “For China, discussing this is meaningless. Any peace plan must indeed fully take into account the views of Ukraine and Europe. This should be similar to the views of the new U.S. Congress.”
Also with the APEC summit in mind, Chinese policymakers will want to see if Trump is willing to strike a bargain to secure quick economic gains, given U.S. voter anger over the cost of living. There is also hope that a Democratic Congress would do more to push back on Trump’s use of tariffs – a tool that typically belongs to the legislative branch, not the executive, under the U.S. system of government.
“If the Democrats can restrain Trump’s impulses to China and other countries in the areas of tariffs and trade, that would be better for China-U.S. relations,” Mu said.
But few in China expect a Democratic-majority Congress to look too much different. “Structural contradictions exist in China-U.S. relations, and both the two parties share negative views on China, for example on national security or high-tech competition,” Mu noted. “These will not change in any particular way due to the outcome of the midterms.”
More broadly, Chinese analysts largely took the U.S. election results as evidence for already-held assumptions about a crumbling U.S. political system. Xinhua’s own original reporting , including on-the-street interviews with voters, portrayed a sense of pessimism and despair. Nearly all the quotes were from voters who expressed doubt that anything would change, regardless of who is in power. One sample: “I have no confidence in any politician, and I don’t think they will focus on what is right for us.”
That was a far cry from the palpable sense of optimism emanating from the Democratic Party as the election results rolled in. But it does fit nearly with China’s preferred thesis that the United States is locked into an irreversible decline.
And whatever Beijing may say about the election being the United States’ “domestic affair,” it will not be lost on Chinese leaders that an unpopular war far from home, and its economic consequences, resulted in severe political punishment for the ruling party. That will factor in to China’s ongoing calculations about what the Iran-U.S. war might imply about Americans’ appetite for intervention in a Taiwan crisis.

Space Exploration Technologies Corp. SPCX shares have fallen 17.8% in the past month even as third-quarter growth, profitability and earnings estimates improved sharply. The pullback has made the stock cheaper, but it has not resolved the debate around capital intensity and execution. Shares are still up 6% over the past three months. That contrast suggests investors are reassessing how much future growth is already reflected in the valuation as spending accelerates.
Third-quarter revenues surged 161.4% year over year to $14.58 billion, while operating income reached $2.79 billion against a $273 million loss a year earlier. Net income improved to $4.40 billion from a $1.05 billion loss. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for the current fiscal year has also moved sharply higher, with the four-week earnings estimate change at 106.2%. Still, a better operating picture must be weighed against an investment program that is expanding faster than internally generated cash.
Connectivity revenues rose 69.5% year over year to $5.25 billion, helped by Starlink consumer subscribers reaching 13.6 million. Enterprise and government revenues climbed 91% to $2.13 billion, broadening the segment beyond consumer subscriptions. Super Intelligence revenues jumped 829.9% to $7.56 billion. New cloud services agreements, the Cursor acquisition and growing Grok adoption drove the increase, while segment operating income turned positive at $431 million after a $1.72 billion loss a year earlier.
Third-quarter capital expenditures reached $19.59 billion, including $16.44 billion for Super Intelligence infrastructure. For the first nine months of 2026, capital spending totaled $48.07 billion versus $13.10 billion of operating cash flow. Management expects fourth-quarter capital expenditures of $35 billion to $40 billion as additional compute capacity comes online. SpaceX had about $89.86 billion in cash and marketable securities at September-end, but the scale of planned investment keeps capital efficiency central to the return outlook.
Starship Flight 14 reached orbit and deployed 26 operational Starlink V3 satellites, but major milestones remain. SpaceX still must demonstrate recovery of both stages, orbital refueling, rapid reusability and a much higher launch cadence to support its broader expansion plans. Rocket Lab Corporation RKLB provides useful launch-sector context through its Electron launch business and developing Neutron vehicle. AST SpaceMobile, Inc. ASTS is building a space-based cellular broadband network for standard smartphones, making it relevant as SpaceX expands Starlink Mobile.
The pullback improves the entry price, but the stock still reflects a difficult balance between fast growth and unusually heavy spending. Sustained returns depend on Starship execution, continued Starlink expansion and profitable utilization of rapidly growing compute capacity. SPCX currently carries a Zacks Rank #3 (Hold). Its Momentum Score of A is its strongest Style Score, while the Value Score of F, Growth Score of C and VGM Score of D point to a less favorable mix across valuation and broader growth characteristics. articles.title_orig: ‘I worry people will forget Hong Kong’: Joshua Wong laments city’s fate from inside maximum security prison
articles.title_zh: ‘I worry people will forget Hong Kong’: Joshua Wong laments city’s fate from inside maximum security prison
articles.content_orig:
Exclusive: pro-democracy activist’s prison letters reveal fascination with AI, brushes with Triads and an appetite for books
Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong sentenced to 10 years in prison in national security case
F rom inside Hong Kong’s oldest maximum security prison, where he swaps books with Triad gang members and studies law, Joshua Wong writes letters like a man desperate to stay connected to the outside world.
Excerpts from his private prison writings reveal the pro-democracy activist asking friends to take screenshots of social media accounts and put questions to AI chatbots on his behalf.
To one acquaintance, he writes about his prison reading habits. “Some of the old-school triad bosses in here have also lent me books,” he says in the letters to friends, seen exclusively by the Guardian. “They read too. One of them lent me Mario Puzo’s The Godfather (lol).”
The 30-year-old Wong, who rose to prominence as the teenage face of Hong Kong’s now-squashed democracy movement, has been imprisoned since November 2020.
On Thursday, he was sentenced to 10 years for foreign collusion , his second conviction under the national security law imposed by Beijing in 2020. Wong pleaded guilty to the charge in September.
Wong is the only pro-democracy activist to be prosecuted twice under the national security legislation. He had been due to be released in January, before the latest prosecution, and will now serve his two sentences concurrently.
Despite spending his 21st, 25th and 30th birthdays in prison, Wong’s letters – written between August and October – show his resolve and continuing concern about Hong Kong’s future.
“The only thing I worry about is that people will forget Hong Kong, and that amid competition and struggles between great powers, they will forget the countless ordinary, unknown people in different places who have paid a price for their beliefs,” he writes.
In Stanley prison, where young inmates use M&Ms as currency, he spends time exercising, learning to play the guitar and teaching English to other prisoners.
“I was teaching English to a Russian,” he says in one letter. “When he asked me what the word ‘totalitarian’ meant, I simply answered, ‘Putin’ (lol)”.
Books appear to be central to his life. His reading list includes Patriot, the memoir of Russian opposition leader, Alexei Navalny, who died in prison in 2024; biographies of Steve Jobs, Nelson Mandela, Benjamin Franklin; and the memoir of former Citibank trader turned YouTuber and inequality campaigner, Gary Stevenson.
On the day of the US presidential election in November 2024, he watched votes come in while holding a copy of JD Vance’s bestselling memoir, Hillbilly Elegy.
Wong gained international attention during the 2014 Umbrella protests , which paralysed the city’s financial centre and galvanised a generation of young people. In October 2014, he appeared – with his trademark black-rimmed spectacles – on the cover of a Time magazine under the headline: “The Face of Protest”.
When protests erupted in 2019 over a proposed extradition bill, Wong was serving a prison sentence for his role in the 2014 demonstrations. He was released at the height of the protests and immediately took to the streets.
In 2020, Beijing said its introduction of the national security law was needed to restore stability to the former British colony, but critics said it gave authorities sweeping powers to crack down on free speech and dissent.
Since then, activists and journalists have been arrested, independent newsrooms closed, and much of the city’s political opposition forced into exile . There have been more than 400 arrests under national security legislation, according to Hong Kong’s security bureau.
“Joshua’s case is part of an attempt to control how my generation’s political history is remembered,” says Frances Hui, a childhood friend and pro-democracy activist in exile.
“For years, people around the world could hear him argue, organise, and explain what he thought Hong Kong’s future should be. Now we can barely hear from him at all.”
In his letters, Wong says Mandela inspired him to study law and he has enrolled in an undergraduate company law course.
He says that he has lost weight, but has a strict routine of pull-ups, squats and pushups. He also reads the Bible and recites passages from the book of Joshua and the Corinthians.
Wong’s childhood friends and fellow activists say the Hong Kong they once fought for no longer exists.
“It is hard to say whose side time is on,” says another childhood friend, who spoke on condition of anonymity for fear of reprisal.
Hui says that Hong Kong authorities had waited nearly five years after the alleged crime to prosecute Wong – just before his release.
“By the time he sees freedom, he is most certainly not going to be the young boy we once remembered,” she says.

articles.title_orig: Putin will not attend Britain's G20 summit, UK PM Burnham says
articles.title_zh: Putin will not attend Britain's G20 summit, UK PM Burnham says
articles.content_orig:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said Vladimir Putin is not invited to the G20 summit in Manchester.
Asked whether the Russian president would be invited to the annual meeting, which the UK is hosting in November 2027, Burnham said "no" because of sanctions against the Kremlin.
The UK has a longstanding policy not to have direct, bilateral engagement with Russian ministers since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022.
But US president Donald Trump has sparked controversy by inviting Putin to this year's G20, which he will host in Miami in December. The Kremlin has not yet said whether Putin will attend.
Russia is a member of the G20 - a group of 19 nations, the European Union and African Union - while Ukraine is not, but the ongoing war in Ukraine has loomed large over recent summits.
Putin has not attended any major global summit since he launched his invasion and ongoing war in Ukraine.
Asked about inviting him to the G20 in Manchester in 2027, Burnham told The Economist he "will not be coming because of an outstanding sanction" on senior Russian figures.
He said the meeting would provide "a real opportunity" to work with Chinese president Xi Jinping on safety regulations for artificial intelligence (AI).
Pressed on whether the UK could bring the US and China around the same table to agree on global AI supervision, Burnham said: "As I sit here today, that feels challenging, but we've got to hold out the need to find global agreements on AI.
"If we don't, the risks of recent times will magnify, they will significantly intensify.
"So you've got to go into it with that aim."
His decision not to include Putin in next year's gathering in Manchester comes after European diplomats refused to stand for an official photo with Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov at the G20 Foreign Ministers' Meeting in October.
The so-called "family photo" would usually include representatives from all nations in attendance, but this year it was cancelled.
The US decision to invite Lavrov in the first place - which itself came after further public rows between Trump and Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky - also attracted criticism.
Discussing Ukraine, UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband later told Lavrov at the summit: "Let me say this directly to the Russian foreign minister: We all know who the aggressor in this war is."
The UK last hosted the G20 summit in 2009. Next year's two-day event will take place in the Manchester Central Convention Centre in Manchester city centre and host thousands of diplomats and delegates, as well as world leaders.
The government has said it will use its G20 presidency in 2027 to "reinforce global economic stability" and "benefit people in every part of the UK".

articles.title_orig: Wendy's rejects $1.4 billion hostile takeover bid, saying it undervalues the company
articles.title_zh: Wendy's rejects $1.4 billion hostile takeover bid, saying it undervalues the company
articles.content_orig:
Wendy's board of directors on Thursday unanimously rejected a $1.4 billion hostile takeover bid from a group of investment firms, saying the offer undervalues the restaurant chain and is not in the best interest of shareholders.
"The Independent Committee thoroughly evaluated this Proposal and unanimously concluded that it substantially undervalues Wendy's standalone prospects and long-term earnings potential," Art Winkleblack, chairman of the board, said in a statement, while also expressing confidence in CEO Bob Wright.
The takeover bid was led by asset management firm Trian Partners, founded by activist investor Nelson Peltz, along with Flynn Group LP, BlueFive Capital and Sixth Street Partners.
The groups are offering $7.35 per share for Wendy's, whose stock traded at $7.75 before markets opened on Thursday. Wendy's confirmed it received the unsolicited offer last month and said it would create an independent board to review the proposal.
Although it remains profitable, Wendy's has faced slowing revenue growth in recent years, and its stock price has slumped nearly 14% over the last 12 months.
In its latest earnings report on Thursday, Wendy's said that U.S. same-restaurant sales decreased 5.7% in the third quarter, compared with the same period last year. The chain reported $547 million in revenue, down from $549.5 million in the year-ago quarter.
Wendy's is losing traction with customers as inflation and rising beef costs force the burger chain to raise prices, the Associated Press reported last week.
The company has also struggled with operational issues, including staffing, employee training, handling drive-thru orders and marketing, Wright said during a call with Wall Street analysts in August. More broadly, he acknowledged that Wendy's must improve the quality of its food to drive business.
"Wendy's has always been known for quality, fresh, never frozen beef, hamburgers made to order, bacon cooked in our restaurants and fresh produce prepared daily," he said. "But over time, we've drifted away from some of the standards that made Wendy's distinctive. While we've maintained core practices in some areas, we've led cost and efficiency drive decisions that weaken that differentiation."
Other businesses across the fast-food industry are also struggling as inflation weighs on customers' wallets. McDonald's reported on Wednesday that it would offer a new array of affordable options next year to boost sales.

articles.title_orig: Bank of England Raises Rates for First Time in Three Years
articles.title_zh: Bank of England Raises Rates for First Time in Three Years
articles.content_orig:
UK hit by first interest rate rise in three years, as Bank predicts inflation will approach 5% by middle of 2027
Andrew Bailey then hints that the Bank could well raise interest rates again, following today’s hike to 4% , unless the Iran war ends.
He tells reporters in London:
double quotation mark Today’s increase should not be seen as the first in an inevitable long sequence of hikes. That is not inevitable.
But unless the conflict in the Middle East is resolved, neither does it seem likely to be the last increase.
Back on Wall Street, the Dow Jones industrial average (DJIA) has slumped by 2.5%, or 1,346 points, as shares retreat sharply.
Both the S&P 500 share index and the tech-focused Nasdaq has hit their lowest levels since late July, and on track for their biggest one-day drop in five months.
Chip giant Nvidia is leading the selloff on the DJIA , down 8%, followed by Goldman Sachs which has dropped by 6.5%.
A December hike in UK interest rates is now “on the table”, argues consultancy Oxford Economics , following today’s rise.
Oxford Economics believes that December’s Monetary Policy Committee meeting “looks like a coin flip”, with oil and natural gas prices set to be the decisive factor.
Their chief UK economist Andrew Goodwin reckons the committee’s messaging was more hawkish than before.
double quotation mark “Higher energy futures prices and more evidence of domestic resilience both increase the risk of second-round effects emerging.
The degree of inflationary pressure already in the system means another hike in December or February is likely.”
America’s technology share index, the Nasdaq Composite, has fallen into correction territory.
The Nasdaq Composite is down 4% today, as tech stocks drop sharply, and is now more than 10% below its record closing high.
Oil and gas aren’t the only volatile elements in the markets today, following the events of the last 48 hours.
Over on Wall Street, Elon Musk’s businesses are being hit in the aftermath of the midterm election results.
Shares in Tesla and SpaceX are both down around 9% in early trading, adding to losses yesterday that wiped billions of dollars off both company’s valuation.
The midterms have been something of a disaster for Musk.
He contributed at least $446m to Republican-aligned Super Pacs and groups over the course of the elections, specifically targeting several key Senate races in an effort to help the Trump administration retain Republican control of Congress – and then watched the Democrats rack up a series of election wins.
Voters across the US also voted for bans or restrictions on datacentre development, in a backlash against AI.
Several economists are arguing that today’s rise in UK interest rates is not the start of a long cycle of rate hikes.
Sanjay Raja , Deutsche Bank’s chief UK economist, says today’s move is an “insurance policy” against the danger ofsecond-round effects (a wage-price spiral), arguing:
double quotation mark Today’s hike merely adds a dose of policy restriction to an already restrictive policy stance. Moreover, with financial conditions having tightened materially since March, the case to go much further isn’t as strong as it may have been in the Bank’s previous hiking cycle back in 2022.
With signs of second-round effects remaining minimal at this juncture, we retain our view for one more hike with Bank Rate peaking at 4.25%. And perhaps the bigger question from today’s decision is whether the next hike comes in December or February. There is a clear risk that the MPC could go earlier – this will be something to watch in the coming weeks and will likely be determined by forthcoming inflation outturns as well as developments in the Middle East (with the last 48 hours delivering some good news on energy price expectations).
Modupe Adegbembo, economist at investment bank Jefferies , believes another hike is likely, but not a foregone conclusion, telling clients:
double quotation mark February is our base case, but the MPC looks willing to pause if the backdrop improves materially.
A resolution to the conflict or a further meaningful stabilisation in energy prices would reduce the need for another move, particularly if second-round effects remain limited. So we think the bias is towards another hike in February, but it remains conditional on the energy shock and evidence of persistence.
Daniel Siluk , head of global short duration & liquidity at Janus Henderson Investors , is also cautious about interpreting today’s decision as the beginning of a prolonged hiking cycle.
double quotation mark The energy shock is lifting headline inflation, but there remains relatively limited evidence that it is becoming embedded in broader wages and prices. At the same time, higher energy bills, elevated mortgage rates and tighter financial conditions are increasingly weighing on household purchasing power and should ultimately slow demand. Andrew Bailey was careful to stress that today’s move should not be viewed as the first in a sequence of increases. Our view is that the Bank is effectively buying some insurance against second-round inflation effects and protecting its inflation-fighting credibility.
One further increase looks increasingly plausible, but the bigger question for markets is whether the considerably longer tightening cycle currently reflected in the curve will ultimately be delivered.
That was the end of the Bank’s press conference – here’s our news story about the interest rate hike:
Q: You say the best thing that can happen is, is to resolve the conflict in the Middle East. Given the events of the last 48 hours, would you make that plea directly to US President Donald Trump or the Republican Party for the sake of the UK economy or global economy? (asks Hannah Brenton of Politico).
Andrew Bailey replies that prime minister Andy Burnham put this pont very clearly in the last 24 hours, speaking at the Commonwealth summit [where the PM said the midterm election results are an “opportunity” to focus on ending the Iran war].
Bailey says he supports Burnham on this issue, explaining:
double quotation mark I mean, he also made the same point about Russia’s illegal invasion of Ukraine.
This is absolutely critically important….
I’m very much speaking in the same vein and very much support what he said.
Q: How mindful of you about the NEET crisis, as you mentionead earlier that lower-paid people who are struggling to find work will be hit the hardest by inflation?
Andrew Bailey replies that the Bank is “very conscious” that there is a section of the population on low pay and section of population that isn’t able to find work.
double quotation mark We’re very conscious of the impact that inflation, particularly energy price inflation or inflation that originates in energy prices, has, so we are very conscious of that.
Q: Under your central projection, inflation returns target in the third quarter of 2028. It will then have been above the 2% target for for all but one of the previous seven years – what does that say about the BoE’s credibility as an inflation-targeting central bank?
Bailey blames the series of shocks that have hit the UK economy, arguing that few people would have predicted in 2020 that we would today be living in a world where there is a major war in the Middle East and in Europe at the same time .
Q: Governor, you said before the budget that fiscal policy needed to be directed towards stability, and be seen by markets as credible – did the chancellor get the message?
Andrew Bailey bristles at the suggestion he was trying to influence John Healey’s first budget, saying:
double quotation mark I’m very careful what I say on fiscal policy. I said nothing on the budget whatsoever.
Bailey then deploys the BoE’s monetary policy remit in his defence, saying it gives the Bank the objective of supporting the economic policies of the government of the day, including the fiscal framework.
double quotation mark I do support it. So there’s nothing more to it t

articles.title_zh: Bring Khazalite might to armies of Order with Regiments of Renown

Bring Khazalite might to armies of Order with Regiments of Renown
For such a stubborn lot, the duardin of the Khazalite Holds work rather well with their Grand Alliance Order allies, and two new Regiments of Renown from their upcoming battletome show you how.
The first, Fjori’s Vengeance, stars the last survivor of Guzanhold and the gaggle of mercenary Fyreslayers he’s gathered to help him wreak ancestral retribution upon those responsible for the magmahold’s fall. As a Grimhold Exile , Fjori is a deadly close combat killer who can normally propel himself to a distant board edge once per game, but now with the Regiment’s new Itinerant Grimmdron rule he can bring the rest of his gang with him too.
Once Per Battle (Army), Deployment Phase
Well used to being outnumbered, Fjori turns the situation to his advantage as he outflanks the foe with his warriors.
Effect: If the Grimhold Exile in this Regiment of Renown has used the ‘Wrathful Wanderer’ ability this battle, remove the other units in this Regiment of Renown from the battlefield and set them up again on the battlefield wholly within 6" of a battlefield edge, wholly within 6" of the Grimhold Exile in this Regiment of Renown and more than 9" from all enemy units. Then, give a unit in this Regiment of Renown 1 grudge mark .
The sudden appearance of tough and dangerous Fyreslayers is a great help to many armies who want to pull enemy troops away from the front line, as it’s pretty hard to ignore someone with the potential to throw out Damage 3 attacks when charging.
Once Per Battle (Army), Deployment Phase
Grimhold Exiles are accustomed to operating alone. They go where they will, and death follows them.
Effect: Remove this unit from the battlefield, then set it up again on the battlefield wholly within 6" of a battlefield edge and more than 9" from all enemy units.
His entourage are equally dangerous and the whole lot can appear from any point near a board edge – great for teaming up with soaring Kharadron Overlords airships or speedy aelven cavalry.
The second Regiment of Renown brings a spot of duardin rune magic to other Order armies courtesy of the eponymous Runewright and his contingent of hardy Khazalite infantry. It’s a sizable force compared to its Grimmdron peers, with 10 Clanshields, 10 Clangunners, the Runewright himself, and an Oathkeeper Cannon to keep enemy heads down.
This Regiment of Renown doubles down on the hardiness of the average duardin and is perfect for less durable armies* who want a hard core to brawl over tricky objectives. The Rune of Stoicism spell is a great little buff that will help your forces stick around a bit longer with Ward 6+, while the Grudgesettlers rule gives them a hefty punch early in the game by starting with an ever-useful grudge token .
The sombre resonance of this rune instils in duardin a stubborn determination.
Declare: Pick the Runewright in this Regiment of Renown to cast this spell, then make a casting roll of 2D6.
Effect: Until the start of your next turn, units in this Regiment of Renown have WARD (6+) while they are wholly within 12" of and visible to this unit.
No matter the grievance, Thengin and his kin are ever ready to mete out retribution.
Effect: Each unit in this Regiment of Renown starts the battle with 1 grudge mark .
If a unit in this Regiment of Renown destroys an enemy unit, you must remove the grudge mark from that friendly unit.
This Regiment of Renown is also a particularly nice way to get some of the lovely new Khazalite Holds miniatures even when you’re not planning to start a full army, as they can be used across the whole spectrum of Grand Alliance Order armies. You get a cannon! We bet the Daughters of Khaine or Idoneth Deepkin would love to have a cannon handy.
Will you be adding a wandering band of hard-headed Khazalites to your army? The Khazalite Holds go on pre-order from Saturday , including Fjori’s Vengeance and the individual units that make up Thengin’s Grudgesettlers.

articles.title_zh: US weekly jobless claims at 57-year lows amid low layoffs
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
WASHINGTON, Nov 5 (Reuters) - The number of Americans filing new claims for unemployment benefits slipped to a 57-year low last week, pointing to labor market resilience, though uncertainty over the drawn-out conflict in the Middle East is constraining hiring.
Other data from the Labor Department on Thursday showed stronger-than-expected growth in worker productivity in the third quarter. The surge in productivity depressed labor costs for the ‌first time in more than a year and reinforced views of policymakers and economists that the labor market was not a source of inflation.
Benign wage inflation gives the Federal Reserve more latitude to focus on ‌rising price pressures stemming from the US-Israeli war with Iran. Anger over the conflict, now in its ninth month, cost President Donald Trump's Republican party control of Congress, with Democrats performing strongly in this week's midterm elections.
Initial claims for state unemployment benefits fell 6,000 to a seasonally adjusted 189,000 for ​the week ended October 31, the Labor Department said. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast 196,000 claims for the latest week.
Claims matched the 189,000 level touched in mid-July, which was the lowest reading since 1969. They have stayed mostly below 200,000 since mid-September. Low layoffs, thanks to strong domestic demand and profit growth, are anchoring the labor market. But some economists viewed the low level of jobless claims as a function of a smaller labor force amid an immigration crackdown, rather than fewer job cuts.
Others believed the labor market could be tightening. The government reported this week that there were 1.06 open jobs for every unemployed person in September, up from 1.02 in August.
No state reported an increase in unadjusted claims in excess of 1,000 last week. A separate ‌report from global outplacement firm Challenger, Gray and Christmas showed US-based employers announced 43,994 ⁠job cuts in October, up 2% from September. Planned layoffs dropped 71% compared to October 2025.
Despite the rise over the month, layoffs were the lowest for any October since 2023. Employers announced plans to hire 444,692 workers last month, a 57% jump from October 2025. Hiring plans were the highest for any October since 2009, and likely mostly seasonal jobs.
"Employers are holding on ⁠to the workers they have heading into the holidays, and the hiring they are announcing is largely short-term, seasonal work," said Andy Challenger, chief revenue officer at Challenger, Gray & Christmas. "Companies want the flexibility to meet holiday demand without adding permanent headcount."
The reluctance to increase permanent hiring means some unemployed people are experiencing long periods of joblessness.
The claims report showed the number of people receiving unemployment benefits after an initial week of aid, a proxy for hiring, increased 23,000 to a still-low seasonally adjusted 1.718 million during the week ended October ​24.
The ​so-called continuing claims, however, do not include some unemployed people, including recent college graduates and others who have little or no work history. ​Some might also have exhausted their eligibility for benefits, limited to 26 weeks in most states, ‌keeping continuing claims at relatively low levels.
The claims report has no bearing on the government's closely watched employment report for October due on Friday as it falls outside the survey period. Nonfarm payrolls likely increased by 65,000 jobs last month after rising 29,000 in September, a Reuters survey of economists showed. The unemployment rate is forecast unchanged at 4.2%. The Chicago Fed is projecting the jobless rate at 4.14%, which would round down to 4.1%.
US stocks were lower. The dollar was steady against a basket of currencies. US Treasury yields fell.
A separate report from the Labor Department's Bureau of Labor Statistics showed nonfarm productivity, which measures hourly output per worker, increased at a 3.6% annualized rate in the third quarter after advancing by an upwardly revised 2.1% pace in the second quarter.
Economists had forecast productivity increasing at a 2.8% rate after a previously reported 1.4% growth pace in the second quarter. Productivity is volatile on a quarter-on-quarter basis. It grew at ‌a 2.1% rate from a year ago. Economists and policymakers are hoping that an artificial intelligence spending blitz will translate into significant productivity ​gains.
"AI has yet to make a noticeable contribution. Productivity gains have been fairly consistent over the past several years," said Stephen Stanley, chief US ​economist at Santander US Capital Markets. "What we have seen is a transformation of the economy that came out ​of the trauma of the pandemic. Businesses had to figure out new ways to operate during the pandemic and many of their improvisations yielded lasting efficiency improvements."
Unit labor costs — the price of ‌labor per single unit of output — fell at a 0.7% rate last quarter. That was ​the first decline since the second quarter of 2025 and followed ​an upwardly revised 1.9% growth pace in the second quarter. The data also showed workers' share of economic output falling to new lows.
Economists had forecast labor costs rising at a 0.6% pace after growing at a previously reported 1.2% rate. Labor costs grew at a 2.4% rate from a year ago. They followed on the heels of data last week showing a moderate increase in the Employment Cost Index, the broadest measure of ​labor costs, in the third quarter. Policymakers and economists have argued that the jobs market ‌was not a source of inflation.
The US central bank last week left its benchmark overnight interest rate in the 3.75%-4.00% range while acknowledging that inflation "remains elevated." Economists expect the Fed to raise borrowing costs ​in December.
"The Fed will take some comfort from continued solid productivity gains and subdued unit labor costs, though any evidence that the job market is starting to tighten would weigh toward additional rate hikes," ​said Sal Guatieri, a senior economist at BMO Capital Markets.

articles.content_orig:
The Signature 27 comes with true flagship specs — and a price that has RAMageddon written all over it.
The Signature 27 comes with true flagship specs — and a price that has RAMageddon written all over it.
Motorola is trying something it hasn’t attempted in the modern smartphone era: to make an all-out flagship slab-style phone.
Previous high-end Edge devices never quite hit the mark , and lacked features that would put it in the highest flagship tiers. The company has had plenty of success with its Razr clamshell foldables, leaning on brand nostalgia and daring to make phones that actually look good. But it’s trying something different with its new Signature line , which until now hasn’t been available in the US. The Signature 27 goes a step further toward premium, daring to take on the likes of the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra. Motorola is leaning into a luxury aesthetic, offering a stacked feature set — with an equally luxurious $1,599 price tag.
It’s a lot to ask for a starting price, but it does get you 512GB of storage and 12GB of RAM, the same as the S26 Ultra’s $1,599, 512GB variant. Samsung does offer a cheaper 256GB configuration for $1,399, though.
We got our first look at the Signature 27 when Motorola previewed it earlier this year , revealing that it would use Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 chipset. The company dropped a few other details, too, like Bang & Olufsen-designed audio, 50-megapixel and 200-megapixel telephoto cameras, and two Pantone color options. Today’s full announcement fills in the gaps. It will come with a 7,000mAh silicon-carbon battery, a 6.8-inch tandem OLED screen, IP68/IP69 ratings for full dust and water resistance, and 12GB of RAM. The Signature 27 will also support the privacy-focused GrapheneOS — a first for Motorola, and for a mainstream phone sold in the US, for that matter.
It’s hard to find fault with the 27’s feature set, aside from the lack of built-in Qi2 magnets, which is a bummer. The tandem OLED display uses two light-emitting panels to reach a peak brightness of 12,000 nits. The more battery efficient dual-layer might mean that the phone can reach its highest brightness setting without drawing too much power and overheating the phone, but we’ll want to see if that bears out in practice.
The camera array features a 50-megapixel Sony Lytia L910 sensor with LOFIC technology , meaning it should deliver plenty of dynamic range. In addition to a 3x 200-megapixel camera and a 50-megapixel ultrawide, there’s also an Event Vision Sensor, or EVS. It’s designed to identify movement on a pixel level, which Motorola says will help “capture fast-moving subjects with greater clarity and precision.”
That Bang & Olufsen audio system includes a redesigned speaker architecture for sound that’s “meant to be felt, not just heard,” according to Motorola’s press release. That’d be quite a feat to pull off with a smartphone audio system and I’m not holding my breath. Elsewhere, the Signature 27 offers up to 90W wired charging and up to 50W wireless charging — though you’ll need to use Motorola’s proprietary wireless charger. But in better news, Motorola is promising seven years of OS upgrades for the Signature 27, putting it right up there with the best support policies from Samsung and Google.
Maybe it’s a case of unlucky timing that Motorola decided to go toe-to-toe with Samsung’s premium flagship just as we started gearing up for RAMageddon: Year Two. Maybe in a few years’ time every flagship phone will cost well over $1,000. But right now, $1.600 is a steep hill to ask people to climb, and the Signature 27 will need to come up with more than just an impressive spec sheet.
And just to prove a point, Motorola is also announcing some updates to its wider ecosystem, too. The new Moto Watch Fit 27 claims up to 12 days of battery life, and the Moto Buds 27 offer Bose ANC with IP57 ratings for both the buds and the case. Motorola isn’t announcing pricing or an exact release date for either in the US, only that they’ll be available in the coming months. Both will arrive in the coming “weeks” in Europe and the UK, where the watch will start at £99.99 (about $134 US) and the buds will cost £179.99 (about $242).
Pre-sales for the Signature 27 start on November 19th in the US; the phone goes on sale November 26th.

articles.title_orig: After Riots and Protests, French Workers Are Going on Strike
articles.title_zh: After Riots and Protests, French Workers Are Going on Strike
articles.content_orig:
PARIS — Riot police clashed with protesters in Lyon on Thursday as a nationwide public sector strike tapped into growing anger over deteriorating services and the rising cost of living.
Paris’ iconic Eiffel Tower was closed because of the strike.
Officers clad in black helmets and protective clothing charged at crowds in Lyon after the demonstrations against rising living costs and in support of the high school protest movement turned violent and fires were set in the streets. Water cannons were also deployed. Some of the protesters wore gas masks and safety glasses as a precaution against tear gas.
Images from Paris showed students and other protesters facing off against riot police.
Police were “keeping the situation under control, but it remains tense,” the French Interior Ministry said in a statement at 1 p.m. local time (7 a.m. ET).
“Several violent acts have been committed as part of the high school student movement,” the statement said. After fireworks were fired at a school near the southern city of Toulouse, a fire broke out “that burned the student services office,” it added.
In the city of Rennes in northwest France, metal pétanque balls were thrown at officers, the statement said, adding that police had been pelted with other projectiles in the cities of Pau and Orleans.
Around 250 rallies against rising living costs had been planned in cities and towns across the country and hundreds of thousands of people would likely turn out, unions said before the events kicked off.
France’s main unions, including the CGT and CNT representing public and private sector workers, and the UNEF, representing students, warned the government of President Emmanuel Macron’s that the country was on the brink or recession.
“Everything is going up except wages and pensions,” they said in a joint statement. “Anger is immense.”
“The situation in this country is fragile. The pressing social and environmental challenges must be addressed without delay,” the statement added.
The movement grew from a student protest over staff shortages at the Antoine de Saint-Exupéry High School in Créteil, a southeastern suburb of Paris. Videos of the blockade spread on social media, and soon protests expanded to high schools across the nation.
As the movement grew, the list of grievances expanded beyond the failings of the public school system to encompass broader economic, political and social dissatisfaction. Soon, university students, teachers, parents and politicians also joined.
Hundreds of thousands of protesters have since taken to the streets as the demonstrations expanded, with participants holding signs criticizing the far-right National Rally party and warning of the risks of climate change and artificial intelligence. A multitude of Palestinian flags have also been seen.
Macron, who will leave office in May, convened a defense ‌and security meeting Wednesday ahead of the protests. Later, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said that 70,000 police officers would be deployed Thursday, backed by armored vehicles, drones and helicopters.
Police have previously been criticized for injuring protesters with heavy-handed tactics. Last month, a 15-year-old was maimed by a sting ball grenade fired by police and a 14-year-old suffered a jaw fracture in a similar incident.
Several other have also suffered life-changing injuries and a 59-year-old man, identified as Christophe M, died Oct. 17 of “a critical cardio-respiratory failing” after leaving Paris’ Place de la République which had been tear-gassed be police. An investigation into his death is ongoing.
Zacharie Petit reported from Paris and Henry Austin from London.
Zacharie Petit is a producer in Paris.
Henry Austin is a senior editor for NBC News Digital based in London.

articles.title_orig: 2026 iPad mini review: Maximizing the mini
articles.title_zh: 2026 iPad mini review: Maximizing the mini
articles.content_orig:
The iPad mini has long felt like a niche product. It has earned a reputation as a quality tablet for people who want something small, comfortable, and portable, but its small screen and comparatively limited processing power have restricted its appeal, making it best suited to watching media or playing games.
With the 2026 version , the iPad mini is more competitive than ever. Its chip is current, its speakers are better, and, most impressively, it trades its 8.3-inch IPS screen for an 8.5-inch OLED that can hold its own against other premium tablets. There isn’t much more you can ask of an iPad this small.
But at just $50 less than the larger, more powerful iPad Air (11-inch) , the iPad mini still has a hard time making a case for itself.
The most immediately noticeable change to the 2026 iPad mini is its display. At 0.2 inches larger than the 2024 iPad mini’s screen, the difference might not sound like much, but it has a meaningful impact on a tablet this small. Beyond providing a bigger view of photos, video content, and lengthy documents, the extra space makes it easier to work with multiple windows, giving you more room to view them and adjust their size and location.
One of our biggest complaints about the prior mini was its bezels, which felt large for a tablet of its size. This time, Apple managed to fit a larger screen in a slightly smaller tablet (7.69 × 5.22 × 0.21 inches and 0.56 pounds for the 2026 mini versus 7.69 × 5.3 × 0.25 inches and 0.65 pounds for the 2024 mini) by reducing the bezels by 24 percent. The result is a streamlined viewing experience that feels more modern and appropriate for a new Apple product.
And you’ll certainly want to watch content on the 2316 × 1512 OLED display, which packs 326 pixels per inch. OLED displays often lack the brightness of their LCD-LED counterparts, but the gap has narrowed in recent years. The new mini is brighter than its IPS-based predecessor, with Apple claiming full-screen brightness of up to 600 nits, compared to 500 nits on the previous model. It’s also much better suited to HDR content, with peak HDR brightness reaching 1,200 nits for highlights and a contrast ratio of 2,000,000:1.
Since content consumption is arguably the mini’s strongest use case, it makes sense for Apple to focus on changes that enhance the viewing experience. Watching shows and movies feels as luxurious as possible on a screen this size, and the mini maximizes its display in nearly all the ways that matter.
I say “nearly” because the mini still has a 60 Hz refresh rate; 120Hz is limited to the iPad Pro . A 120 Hz refresh rate makes little difference when watching most shows or movies, but it can make some tasks, such as scrolling through long documents, look smoother. Still, the difference is less noticeable on a smaller screen.
Overall, the refresh rate didn’t feel like a drawback during regular use. Apple has gone a step further , noting that OLEDs typically have faster response times than IPS displays. That’s generally true when discussing gray-to-gray (GtG) response times. However, moving picture response time (MPRT) can be a better indicator of potential persistence-related motion blur, including during scrolling, because it measures how long an image remains visible on the display, contributing to blur as your eyes track moving content. GtG, by contrast, measures how quickly individual pixels transition between shades. Slower pixel transitions can create motion artifacts such as ghosting.
According to Blur Busters’ MPRT Indicator , the mini has an MPRT of about 17 ms, about what I’d expect from a 60 Hz IPS display. Anyone who needs a high-refresh screen will still want to look at the Pro series.
One feature the mini borrows from the iPad Pro but that other iPads lack is the option for nano-texture glass, which is designed to reduce glare. It costs an extra $100 and is only available on the 256GB and 512GB versions of the mini.
The 2024 mini debuted with a year-old chip, but this year’s model sports Apple’s latest mobile processor. The 2026 mini makes a considerable jump from the A17 Pro, a 3-nanometer, iPhone 15 Pro-era chip from 2023, to the A20 Pro, a 2-nanometer chip that debuted in the new iPhone 18 Pro .
The newer chip has 50 percent more memory bandwidth, which significantly boosts graphics performance. It’s also up to 60 percent faster.
I tested the 512GB version of the iPad Mini, which, like the 128GB and 256GB versions, features a seven-core integrated GPU. The 512GB model, however, gets a bump from five CPU cores to six and doubles the number of 16-core Neural Engines from one to two, promising better performance in on-device AI applications, such as image generation.
I don’t expect many people to run particularly intensive workloads on a tablet this small. Still, tasks such as photo editing, light video editing, and juggling many open applications felt smooth. The performance boost makes the iPad mini much more powerful than the standard iPad 11 , which uses an A16 processor. The iPad Pro (M5) and the iPad Air (M4), however, remain better equipped for demanding workloads such as video editing and 3D rendering.
Siri AI is still in beta, so we won’t cover that in this review. But the tablet supports features under the Apple Intelligence umbrella, including various generative AI capabilities. Tasks like removing objects from photos, changing a photo’s perspective, or extending a photo’s borders should take roughly the same amount of time on the 512GB iPad mini as they do on the iPhone 18 Pro. In my experience, that’s usually about 20 seconds.
The mini is surprisingly loud. Its speakers are powerful enough to make TV dialogue easy to hear, even with my noisy heater running in the background.
The tablet has two woofers designed to deliver higher volume and stronger bass than the prior mini. A pair of custom-designed tweeters between the tablet’s glass and aluminum enclosure are intended to improve the clarity of higher frequencies.
You won’t get the deepest bass or the crispest high notes, but the speakers surpassed my expectations when playing music. I didn’t immediately feel the need to connect the iPad to dedicated speakers.
And the mini pulls this off without any visible speaker holes in its chassis.
That detail helped the mini earn the first IP67 rating for an iPad. The Ingress Protection rating means the device is “dust-tight” and “protected against the effects of temporary immersion in water,” according to the International Electrotechnical Commission .
The 2026 mini has the same 12 MP front and back cameras as its 2024 predecessor, but the front-facing camera has moved from one of the shorter sides to one of the longer sides. This took some getting used to for FaceTiming and selfies. Holding the tablet in portrait orientation now places you off-center in the frame, while holding it in landscape mode to FaceTime on the go quickly became uncomfortable. The new location was fine when I could sit down and prop the tablet on a stand.
Another addition is the back camera’s Adaptive True Tone flash, which Apple markets as a way to quickly scan documents. When the Camera app identifies a document, such as a piece of paper or a book, it automatically adjusts which of the camera’s LEDs light up to minimize shadows and produce clearer text.
When I used the tablet’s camera to photograph text on both a piece of paper and a book, it quickly used machine learning to identify them as documents. A pop-up appeared, offering the option to “Scan Document”; selecting it allowed me to automatically take a picture of just the document. It’s not a feature many people will use regularly, but when the need arises, it makes capturing a sharp, detailed image of text considerably easier.

articles.content_orig:
Discord is moving its apps fully over to the Rust programming language.
Discord is moving its apps fully over to the Rust programming language.
Discord is finally giving up on Electron, the cross-platform framework that lets developers build desktop apps using web technologies. Electron web apps are notoriously heavy on system resources, and Discord is now moving its desktop app fully to Rust — a modern programming language designed for speed and memory safety.
“We’ve been early adopters of Rust since 2018 and a lot of our infra, voice tech, and even some of the current client is already Rust, the holy grail was getting the whole client there,” explains Discord chief technology officer Stanislav Vishnevskiy in a post on X . “That means Electron goes away, and so does React Native, mobile keeps native UI but shares app code with desktop via Rust.”
Vishnevskiy also shared an image of the Discord Windows client using just 290MB of RAM, which is a clear improvement as you only have to participate in a few servers and RAM usage can easily hit 1GB or more using the current Windows app.
It’s not clear when Discord will make the full switch over to Rust, but Vishnevskiy says the company “hope to get it into testing with users soon.”

articles.title_orig: Finnish court jails captain and crew member for 'aggravated criminal damage' over Baltic cable sabotage
articles.title_zh: Finnish court jails captain and crew member for 'aggravated criminal damage' over Baltic cable sabotage
articles.content_orig:
A Finnish court on Thursday convicted the Russian captain and a senior crew member of the cargo ship Fitburg for damaging two undersea telecommunications cables in the Gulf of Finland last year.
The Helsinki District Court found the two defendants guilty of "aggravated criminal damage."
It said in a statement that they had intentionally dragged the ship's anchor along the seabed for around 130 kilometers (81 miles).
The captain was sentenced to three and a half years in jail, while the crew member, an Azerbaijani citizen, was sentenced to two years and 10 months.
They were also ordered to jointly pay around €1.9 million ($2.1 million) in damages, the Reuters news agency reported, with the captain to pay about €85,000 more.
The defendants denied any wrongdoing and have challenged Finland's jurisdiction in the case.
Finnish authorities seized the vessel on December 31 on suspicion that it had damaged cables linking Finland 's capital, Helsinki, and Tallinn, Estonia.
Finnish police at the time said the ship had been dragging its anchor for hours when it was discovered in Finland's exclusive economic zone.
The Fitburg and its 14-member crew had been en route to the port of Haifa, Israel, from the Russian city of St. Petersburg when the incident occurred.
Finland has stepped up efforts to protect its undersea infrastructure following a series of incidents involving cables and pipelines in the Baltic Sea since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
